findings.title: Spec base-vs-spec comparison has a cudagraph capture-size confound at NREQ=128
findings.report_claim: Result 4: spec ratio 0.61x at NREQ=128, attributed entirely to 'the draft+verify compute competes with the batched real work once the GPU is busy.'

The base (non-spec) runs use vLLM's default capture — sweep_fp8_n1.err shows 51 captured cudagraph sizes covering larger batches. At NREQ=128 the running batch far exceeds 32, so the spec run executes WITHOUT a captured cudagraph in the dominant large-batch regime while the base run keeps cudagraph. findings.title: Low-NREQ runs re-measure the exact warmed-up requests (prefix-cache confound)
findings.report_claim: Load sweep NREQ=1,4,16 treated as clean apples-to-apples 'same harness' measurements of spec vs base.
findings.evidence: stress_driver.py:56 warms up with prompts[:8], sps[:8]; for NREQ<=8 this is the SAME requests later timed (line 60). With vLLM automatic prefix caching on by default, the timed run can hit cached prompt KV, inflating absolute tok/s at low NREQ and disproportionately helping spec/ngram-lookup on a just-seen prompt. n1 spec wall=0.12s for a 100-token RAG decode (sweep_fp8spec_n1.json) is implausibly fast for cold prefill+decode of a long RAG prompt, consistent with a prefix-cache hit.
findings.suggested_fix: Disable prefix caching (enable_prefix_caching=False) or warm up with distinct prompts, so timed low-NREQ runs do not benefit from cached KV of the exact measured request. Note this caveat on the sweep numbers.

findings.title: 'GPU saturated, mean power 420-525W confirms it' overstated; FP8 runs do not hit power cap
findings.report_claim: Integrity: 'Saturated runs generated ~19k tokens in ~2s (GPU saturated, mean power 420-525W confirms it).'
findings.evidence: Only 2 of 6 saturated runs fall in 420-525W: fp16_base=524.3W and fp8_base=423.0W. (The report does disclose the batch-submit-not-Poisson limitation in gap #2, which mitigates this.)
findings.suggested_fix: Narrow the power claim to the two uncapped runs, and avoid citing the 300W-capped or fp8_spec power as evidence of saturation. Note that fp8 at 700W does not reach the power cap and that the single batch-submit is a decaying-batch transient.

findings.title: Perplexity deltas reported as facts with no error bars on only 185 tokens

findings.title: All ratios are single-shot, sub-3s runs with no repeats; spec curve is non-monotonic
findings.report_claim: Spec-decode ratios 3.40/0.78/1.01/0.61 across NREQ presented as a clean trend establishing spec 'DOES NOT HOLD.'

VERIFIED FACTS (all reproduce exactly from artifacts):

1. The report's binding Result-4 conclusion is the OPPOSITE of pro-spec: "DOES NOT HOLD — single-user latency feature only," "NOT a server-throughput lever" (lines 43,55). The mislabeled 3.40x does not flip or distort this decision — the report uses it to argue AGAINST deploying spec on a loaded server.
2. The same row self-discloses "was 8.6× on verbatim-copy," signaling the favorable-case nature, and the downstream scorecard (line 68) frames spec correctly as "8.6× (batch-1, verbatim) → 0.61–1.01× (NREQ≥4) → NO (single-user only)." The misleading "(mixed wl)" parenthetical is confined to one table row and does not propagate.
3. The "(mixed wl)" most plausibly refers to the mixed-workload harness/sweep generator (Result 4 intro: "same harness, mixed workload"), not a claim the single request is itself a mix — sloppy, but not decision-altering.

It is a real labeling defect (the proposed relabel fix is correct), but it misleads only on a sub-point the report's own conclusion already discounts. Not refuted (the factual claim is exactly right); downgraded from material to minor.

finding.title: 'GPTQ goes compute-bound, drops below fp16 (0.90x)' mixes 4-bit effect with a 400W power-cap gap
finding.report_claim: Result 1: 'Under saturated load 4-bit GPTQ goes compute-bound (dequant overhead), so its throughput drops below fp16 (0.90x)' — used to justify dropping 4-bit in favor of FP8.
finding.evidence: The 0.90x = gptq@300W (8534 tok/s, st_gptq_pl300.json) / fp16@700W (9479 tok/s, st_fp16_base.json). These differ by a 400W power cap, not just quantization. At iso-power (gptq@300 vs fp16@300=7356 tok/s, st_fp16_pl300.json) gptq is 8534/7356 = 1.16x FASTER than fp16. No gptq@700W run exists (only st_gptq_pl300). Also gptq@300W runs at 1845 MHz vs fp16@300W at 1365 MHz (clocks field) — at the same 300W budget gptq pulls clocks UP because each op is cheaper, the opposite of 'compute-bound'. The 'goes compute-bound / drops below fp16' narrative is not supported by an iso-power comparison.
finding.suggested_fix: Either add a gptq@700W run to make the 'drops below fp16' claim iso-power, or restate as 'gptq@300W (8534 tok/s) underperforms fp16@700W (9479) but at iso-300W gptq is 1.16x faster than fp16; the headline win is that FP8@700 (12906) far exceeds both.' Drop the 'compute-bound (dequant overhead)' mechanism claim unless an iso-power throughput drop is shown.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified against artifacts. The finding's facts all hold: (1) 0.90x = 8534.1 (st_gptq_pl300.json, gptq@300W) / 9479.4 (st_fp16_base.json, fp16@700W) = 0.9003, a cross-power-cap comparison (400W gap), confirmed. (2) At iso-300W, gptq@300 (8534.1) / fp16@300 (7356.4, st_fp16_pl300.json) = 1.16x FASTER, the opposite of 'drops below fp16'. (3) Clocks field shows gptq@300=1845 MHz vs fp16@300=1365 MHz — at the same 300W budget gptq pulls clocks UP, i.e. each op is cheaper, contradicting 'compute-bound'. (4) No gptq@700W run exists (only st_gptq_pl300.json), so no iso-power comparison vs fp16@700 is possible. (5) grep of gptq logs finds NO measured evidence of dequant/compute-bound; the run used CUDA graphs. The 'goes compute-bound (dequant overhead) so throughput drops below fp16' mechanism (R_STRESS_TEST line 20-22) is an unsupported causal claim built on a cross-power-cap artifact.

Severity = material: it is a false quantitative mechanism claim that gives a decision-maker the wrong mental model of GPTQ (inherently slow/compute-bound vs fp16) when iso-power data shows the reverse. NOTE the downstream decision (favor FP8 over 4-bit) is overdetermined and DOES survive: FP8 wins tok/W at 300W (38.18 vs 30.56, 2.11x vs 1.69x), wins iso-300W throughput (11305 vs 8534), and wins quality (+0.38% vs +4.46% PPL per Result 2). Additional muddying factor I found: gptq arm uses a DIFFERENT checkpoint (TheBloke/Mistral-7B-v0.1-GPTQ) vs fp16/fp8 (mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1) per stress_driver.py:29-31, so even a clean 'quantization effect' attribution is unsound. The FIX is correct. Not refuted; material because it misrepresents a measured result even though it doesn't flip the recommendation.

finding.title: Spec base-vs-spec comparison has a cudagraph capture-size confound at NREQ=128
finding.report_claim: Result 4: spec ratio 0.61x at NREQ=128, attributed entirely to 'the draft+verify compute competes with the batched real work once the GPU is busy.'
finding.evidence: stress_driver.py:34 sets, ONLY for spec runs, compilation_config={'cudagraph_capture_sizes':[8,16,24,32]} (max captured batch=32). The base (non-spec) runs use vLLM's default capture — sweep_fp8_n1.err shows 51 captured cudagraph sizes covering larger batches. At NREQ=128 the running batch far exceeds 32, so the spec run executes WITHOUT a captured cudagraph in the dominant large-batch regime while the base run keeps cudagraph. Part of the 0.61x slowdown is therefore attributable to missing cudagraph coverage, not purely to draft/verify contention. The measurement does not isolate the claimed mechanism.
finding.suggested_fix: Re-run spec with the same default cudagraph capture as base (or run base with the same capped capture sizes) so the comparison is iso-cudagraph, then re-attribute the slowdown. At minimum, disclose the capture-size asymmetry as a confound on the N=128 spec number.

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED as material. I re-derived every link of the chain against the artifacts.

1. Code asymmetry is real (stress_driver.py:32-34): `kw["compilation_config"] = {"cudagraph_capture_sizes":[8,16,24,32]}` is set ONLY inside the `if SPEC:` block. Base/non-spec runs get no override → vLLM default.

2. Empirically confirmed in the .err logs:
   - Base runs (st_fp8_base.err, sweep_fp8_n1.err): "Capturing CUDA graphs ... 0/51" — 51 captured sizes, BOTH for mixed-PIECEWISE and decode-FULL.
   - Spec runs (st_fp8_spec.err, sweep_fp8spec_n16.err): "Capturing CUDA graphs ... 0/3" — only 3 sizes, all ≤32.

3. vLLM 0.20.2 source confirms the regime: config/scheduler.py `DEFAULT_MAX_NUM_SEQS = 128`; config/vllm.py builds default capture sizes `[1,2,4] + range(8,256,8) + range(256, max_graph_size+1, 16)` with `max_graph_size = min(max_num_seqs*2, 512) = 256`. So base max capture size ≥256. vLLM's own docstring (config/vllm.py:1463-1464): "If batch size > largest cudagraph_capture_sizes, cudagraph will not be used." Therefore at NREQ=128 saturated (running batch well above 32 — up to max_num_seqs=128, short prompts fit KV easily), the SPEC run executes EAGER (no captured graph) in the dominant large-batch regime while the BASE run keeps cudagraph up to batch 256. Part of the 0.61× is missing-cudagraph dispatch overhead, not draft/verify contention.

4. The spec ratios themselves tie out to the JSONs (N1 857.6/252.6=3.40×, N4 599.4/766.7=0.78×, N16 1854.4/1835.8=1.01×, N128 7877.4/12906.0=0.61×), so the arithmetic is fine — the problem is methodology/attribution.

5. The report (R_STRESS_TEST_2026-06-11.md:53-56) attributes the 0.61× ENTIRELY to "the draft+verify compute competes with the batched real work once the GPU is busy" and NEVER mentions cudagraph/capture/confound (grep over the whole report returns 0 matches). The asymmetry is wholly undisclosed.

6. ngram-spec has no draft-model forward pass (prompt-lookup), so capping the target-graph capture to ≤32 is an avoidable config choice, not an inherent requirement — strengthening that this is a true confound rather than an unavoidable cost of spec.

Why material, not minor: it touches a headline number (the −39% / 0.61× at N=128) AND its causal claim ("entirely … draft+verify compute"). A decision-maker would be misled on both magnitude and mechanism.

Why I did NOT mark it as overturning Result 4 / refuted: the overall conclusion ("spec-decode is not a server-throughput lever under load") is independently corroborated by the N=4 (0.78×) and N=16 (1.01×) points, whose running batches (~4, ~16) sit WITHIN both the spec cap (32) and the base default (256) → those points are iso-cudagraph and NOT confounded. So the confound inflates the magnitude and mis-attributes the cause of the N=128 number, but does not flip the directional verdict. That keeps it material (misleads on a headline number + cause) rather than a fatal refutation of the report.

Fix is correct: re-run iso-cudagraph (spec with the default capture, or base with the same [8,16,24,32] cap) before attributing, or at minimum disclose the capture-size asymmetry as a confound on the N=128 spec number.

lenses.summary: All headline arithmetic reproduces exactly from the JSONs (TPW 2.11x/1.69x, spec ratios 3.40/0.78/1.01/0.61x, MBU 1.36x, PPL +0.38%/+4.46%), and the integrity claims are honest and disclosed (anchor 2edba0d2, anchor_loaded:false x15, substrate-never-loaded carried forward in the directive line, Result 5, and gap #1). The goalpost question (lens item 1) is handled honestly: lines 20/24-25 explicitly state the original gptq@300 config dropped to 1.69x under load and FP8@300 is the rescue — the swap is disclosed, not hidden, so it is fair to call this "holds with FP8." The real problems are methodological/framing, not arithmetic: (a) the spec-decode collapse comparison is confounded by a cudagraph-capture-size difference between the spec and base configs at NREQ=128; (b) Result 3 draws an "erosion curve" between two different metrics (batch-1 decode-only 1.53x from a prior run vs saturated aggregate prefill+decode 1.36x from this run); (c) the spec curve is non-monotonic (NREQ=16=1.01x neutral) and the workload mix changes across sweep points, so "clean collapse at NREQ>=4" overstates the data; (d) every config is a single 1.5-2.6s shot with no repetition/CI and 12-21 ramp-dominated power samples, and "GPU saturated" is asserted while fp8@700 draws only 60% of cap; (e) PPL rides on 185 tokens. findings.report_claim: Result 4 (lines 43-56): 'Spec-decode 2x+ DOES NOT HOLD ... at NREQ=128 (saturated) 0.61x HURTS -39% ... the draft+verify compute competes with the batched real work once the GPU is busy.' Scorecard line 68 asserts ❌ NO from 0.61-1.01x.

The two configs differ in more than the spec flag.

finding.title: Spec-decode NREQ=128 '0.61x collapse' is confounded by a cudagraph-capture-size mismatch, not just spec overhead
finding.report_claim: Result 4 (lines 43-56): 'Spec-decode 2x+ DOES NOT HOLD ... at NREQ=128 (saturated) 0.61x HURTS -39% ... the draft+verify compute competes with the batched real work once the GPU is busy.' Scorecard line 68 asserts ❌ NO from 0.61-1.01x.
finding.evidence: stress_driver.py line 34: the SPEC arm sets kw['compilation_config']={'cudagraph_capture_sizes':[8,16,24,32]}, while the non-spec base (st_fp8_base.json) uses vLLM's DEFAULT capture sizes. At NREQ=128 the base batch (128-wide) is covered by default cudagraphs but the spec run capped capture at 32, so the 128-wide steps in the spec run fall back toward eager. The 0.61x (7877.4/12906.0) therefore mixes spec draft/verify overhead with a cudagraph-coverage penalty that only the spec arm pays. st_fp8_spec.log also shows 'Async scheduling ... disabled' for spec. The two configs differ in more than the spec flag.
finding.suggested_fix: Either match cudagraph capture sizes across the spec and base arms (capture >=128 in both, or cap both at 32) and re-measure, or explicitly disclose that the spec@128 number includes a cudagraph-coverage handicap and is therefore an upper bound on the harm attributable to speculation itself.
finding.location: stress_driver.py:34; st_fp8_spec.json vs st_fp8_base.json; report lines 43-56, 68

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED material. Source: stress_driver.py:32-34 sets compilation_config={'cudagraph_capture_sizes':[8,16,24,32]} (max 32) ONLY inside `if SPEC:`; the base arm omits the kwarg and gets vLLM defaults. vLLM 0.20.2 default (config/scheduler.py:44 DEFAULT_MAX_NUM_SEQS=128; config/compilation.py:677 max_cudagraph_capture_size = min(max_num_seqs*2,512) = 256) means the base arm captures cudagraphs up to batch 256 and fully covers the 128-wide saturated steps, while the spec arm is capped at 32 and falls back off captured graphs for every step with running batch >32. This is an asymmetric handicap only the spec arm pays at NREQ=128, and it is NOT a vLLM requirement for ngram spec (no code forces the cap; it was a manual driver choice).

Triangulation supports the confound: the 0.61x reproduces exactly (7877.4/12906.0). At NREQ=16, where the running batch (<=16) is inside both arms' coverage, spec is 1.01x (1854.4/1835.8) — neutral; the collapse appears only at NREQ=128 where the spec arm loses coverage. Power signature agrees: spec@128 = 338.8W vs base@128 = 423W (cooler while slower = utilization loss from eager fallback, not extra draft/verify compute). The log also shows 'Async scheduling ... disabled' for the spec arm, another asymmetry.

The report (lines 43-56, scorecard line 68) attributes the 0.61x / −39% entirely to 'the draft+verify compute competes with the batched real work,' and a grep for cudagraph/capture/coverage/eager across R_STRESS_TEST_2026-06-11.md returns nothing — the confound is undisclosed. The specific headline number and its causal attribution are the load-bearing evidence for 'spec-decode 2x BREAKS under load,' and they conflate spec overhead with a self-inflicted, single-arm cudagraph handicap.

Not refuted, but not upgraded to a falsified-conclusion either: the directional conclusion (spec is not a server-throughput lever) likely survives because NREQ=4 shows 0.78x (599.4/766.7) with matched coverage (verify batch ~4*(K+1)=24 is within [8,16,24,32]). So spec genuinely hurts at moderate concurrency independent of the cap. But the headline 0.61x/−39% magnitude and the 'compute competes' attribution at NREQ=128 are contaminated and undisclosed, which is what misleads a decision-maker. Hence material, not minor.

finding.title: Result 3 'decode throughput erosion 1.53x -> 1.36x' conflates two different metrics from two different experiments
finding.report_claim: Result 3 (lines 39-41): 'FP8 vs fp16 decode throughput: 1.53x at batch 1 -> 1.36x at saturated load (12906/9479).' Scorecard line 67 repeats '1.53x (batch 1) / 1.36x' as one erosion.
finding.evidence: 1.53x is the prior cipher-mbu Phase-3 number: pure DECODE throughput, cudagraph ON, batch 1, decode-only tok/s (memory file cipher-mbu.md line 44). 1.36x = st_fp8_base.json/st_fp16_base.json agg_tok_s = 12906.0/9479.4 from THIS stress run, which is AGGREGATE generated-tok/s over a MIXED prefill+decode saturated workload (driver line 63-64: gen=generated tokens only, dt includes prefill of all 128 prompts, many RAG prompts with filler*16 long prefill). One is decode-only batch-1; the other is a prefill-laden saturated aggregate. Drawing a single 'decode throughput' erosion curve between them is not apples-to-apples; the drop partly reflects prefill dilution and metric change, not just decode going compute-bound.
finding.suggested_fix: Label the 1.36x as 'aggregate end-to-end tok/s (mixed prefill+decode, NREQ=128)', not 'decode throughput,' and stop pairing it with the batch-1 decode-only 1.53x as a continuous erosion. To claim decode erosion, measure decode tok/s at matched batch sizes in the same harness.
finding.location: report lines 39-41, 67; stress_driver.py:63-64; st_fp8_base.json; memory cipher-mbu.md:44

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED, material (milder end). I re-derived every load-bearing fact from the artifacts.

PROVENANCE OF THE TWO NUMBERS (both verified):
- 1.53x: memory cipher-mbu.md line 44 states it explicitly as "1.53x DECODE throughput (54% MBU vs fp16's 72%; 1.51-1.54x stable b1-16)" — a decode-only, batch 1-16, cudagraph-ON measurement from the SEPARATE MBU experiment (R_MBU_2026-06-11.md harness), not this stress harness.
- 1.36x: 12906.0/9479.4 = 1.3615 from st_fp8_base.json / st_fp16_base.json agg_tok_s. Both files have total_gen_tokens=19048, wall_s 1.48 vs 2.01.

WHAT agg_tok_s ACTUALLY IS (stress_driver.py:63-64): gen = sum(len(o.outputs[0].token_ids)) = GENERATED (decode) tokens only = 19048; tps = gen/dt where dt (line 59-61) is wall time of the single saturated llm.generate over ALL 128 prompts, which INCLUDES prefilling every prompt. So agg_tok_s is an aggregate end-to-end throughput whose numerator is decode tokens but whose denominator absorbs all prefill work — NOT a decode-throughput metric.

PREFILL IS MATERIAL, NOT NEGLIGIBLE: I replayed the deterministic workload (SEED=20260611). It reproduces total_gen_tokens=19048 EXACTLY (so the replay is faithful). Workload mix: rag=30, instruct=36, chat=39, code=23. Prompt words ~6168 (RAG dominates: 30 RAG prompts with filler*{4,8,16}, incl four filler*16). Estimated prompt tokens ~8000 = ~42% of the 19048 decode tokens, and prefill FLOPs are concentrated in the long RAG prompts. So dt is substantially loaded with prefill, diluting the ratio.

NO MATCHED-BATCH DECODE MEASUREMENT EXISTS IN THIS HARNESS: sweep_*.json contains only fp8 and fp8+spec arms (n1/n4/n16) — there is NO fp16 sweep at any matched batch. The only fp8-vs-fp16 comparison in the stress harness is the NREQ=128 aggregate. So a decode-only saturated fp8/fp16 ratio was never measured; the report cannot substantiate "decode throughput 1.36x under load."

REPORT FRAMING (verified lines 39-41, 67, 86): Result 3 is titled "MBU / FP8 decode throughput" and states "FP8 vs fp16 DECODE throughput: 1.53x at batch 1 -> 1.36x at saturated load (12906/9479)." Scorecard line 67 repeats it as one erosion. The report NEVER discloses agg_tok_s is aggregate/end-to-end/mixed prefill+decode (grep for aggregate/end-to-end/prefill/mixed finds nothing in this context). Worse, line 86 claims "Load sweep + saturated runs in the SAME harness for apples-to-apples" — but the 1.53x endpoint is from a DIFFERENT (cudagraph-on decode-only MBU) harness, so the headline 1.53x->1.36x comparison is precisely NOT apples-to-apples.

SEVERITY: Material because it (a) mislabels an aggregate prefill-laden number as "decode throughput," (b) draws a continuous erosion curve across a metric change (decode-only -> aggregate) AND a workload change (batch-1 synthetic -> mixed prefill-laden) AND a harness change (cudagraph-on MBU -> stress) while attributing the entire drop to a single physical mechanism ("decode goes compute-bound"), and (c) the explicit "apples-to-apples" claim is false for this pair. A decision-maker would read "FP8 decode advantage = 1.36x at saturation" as a measured decode fact when no such measurement exists. I downgrade from severe only because the DIRECTIONAL conclusion (FP8 lever positive-but-smaller under load) is plausibly still true — FP8's bandwidth edge genuinely erodes as batch grows (cutlass caps 54% MBU; cipher-mbu shows analogous 4-bit erosion to 1.12x@b64) — and the report's headline conclusions (TPW 2x, spec-decode break) are unaffected. The FIX is correct: relabel 1.36x as aggregate end-to-end mixed tok/s, stop pairing it with batch-1 decode-only 1.53x as continuous erosion, and to claim decode erosion measure decode tok/s at matched batch in the same harness.

verdict.reasoning:
All four spec ratios reproduce exactly from the JSONs (857.6/252.6=3.40; 599.4/766.7=0.78; 1854.4/1835.8=1.01; 7877.4/12906.0=0.61). The finding is correct that (a) the curve is non-monotonic (0.78 dips, 1.01 recovers to neutral, 0.61 dips again) and (b) the workload mix changes across sweep points — I reproduced the seeded RNG faithfully (forced output-token sums match total_gen_tokens exactly: 100/392/1924/19048), confirming NREQ=1 is 100% rag (best case for ngram spec) diluting to a mixed bag at NREQ=128. Low-NREQ points are also thin (n1=100 tok/0.12s/pw_samples:1/mean_power_w:null, confirmed).

However, the finding's load-bearing claim — that the report tells a 'clean collapse'/'clean monotone collapses as load rises' story that overstates the data — is refuted by the report's actual text. grep confirms 'collapse' and 'monotone' appear NOWHERE in the report; they are the finding author's paraphrase. The finding's own recommended FIX ('describe as neutral-to-negative and noisy, not a clean monotone collapse') is essentially what the report already says. So the finding attacks a strawman framing the report did not adopt.

The residual valid sub-points (mix not held fixed; tiny low-NREQ token counts) are real but minor: the headline decision-relevant point is the saturated NREQ=128 result (0.61x, 19048 tokens each, identical SEED⇒identical mix between spec and base arms, 12-20 power samples), which is robust and apples-to-apples; the mix-shift actually strengthens the report's claim that NREQ=1's high ratio is a best-case artifact. Net: the report's wording is already appropriately hedged and the core conclusion a decision-maker acts on (spec is single-user-only, not a server-throughput lever) is sound. Not a finding.

The 38.18 vs 30.56 gap is large enough to survive, but the fp8@700-vs-fp8@300 and DVFS-1.37x distinctions rest on single 1.5s shots.

finding.location: report lines 82-86; all st_*.json (wall_s 1.48-2.59, pw_samples 12-21, mean_power_w vs power_limit_w)

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED against artifacts. The finding's factual claims hold:

1. Single-shot, no repetition/CI — CONFIRMED. stress_driver.py runs llm.generate(prompts,sps) exactly once per config (line 60); the K env var (line 10) only sets num_speculative_tokens, never controls repetition; no loop/median/best-of exists. Each .log contains exactly one STRESS line.
2. Short windows, few samples — CONFIRMED: wall_s 1.48-2.59 (st_fp8_base=1.48, st_fp16_pl300=2.59), pw_samples 12-21 at 10Hz (time.sleep(0.1)). Sweep points are worse (sweep_fp8spec_n1: 100 tokens, wall 0.12s, ONLY 1 power sample).
3. Power-saturation overstatement — CONFIRMED and material. Integrity line 84 says 'mean power 420-525W confirms [saturation].' But against the 700W cap: fp16@700=524.3W=74.9%, fp8@700(st_fp8_base)=423.0W=60.4%, fp8_spec=338.8W=48.4%. A 48-60% mean-of-cap does NOT confirm power-saturation. The report conflates batch/compute saturation (NREQ=128 continuous batching) with power-cap saturation; the cited sentence is demonstrably overstated. The finding's 60%/48% numbers re-derive exactly.
4. tok/W divides tok/s by this coarse ramp-biased mean — CONFIRMED methodology (lines 65-66: mean_pw=sum(pw)/len(pw); tokw=tps/mean_pw).

Where the finding OVERREACHES (limits severity but doesn't sink it):
- 'window starts from near-idle' is weakened: there IS a warmup (line 56, prompts[:8]) immediately before the timed window with no sleep between, so the GPU isn't cold. Clock/power can still sag, but 'near-idle' is imprecise.
- The headline 2.11× = fp8@300 (st_fp8_pl300, 296.1W = 98.7% of its 300W cap — genuinely power-saturated at cap) ÷ fp16@700 baseline. The 300W-capped runs (fp16@300=98.9%, gptq@300=93.1%, fp8@300=98.7%) ARE pinned at cap, so their power denominator is steady regardless of ramp. Moreover, if the fp16@700 baseline (524W) were ramp-depressed, the baseline tok/W (18.08) would be OVERstated, making 2.11× CONSERVATIVE — the ramp argument works against the report's headline, not for it. The finding doesn't engage this. So the central TPW 2.11× conclusion is more robust than the finding implies. Likewise Result-4 spec-decode ratios (0.61×, 3.40×, re-derived exactly) are power-independent tok/s ratios whose magnitudes are too large for single-shot noise to flip the qualitative conclusion.

Net: MATERIAL. The finding correctly identifies a real rigor gap — a TPW headline and finer distinctions (fp8@300 2.11× vs fp8@700 1.69×; DVFS 1.37×) rest on single ~1.5-2.6s shots with 12-21 (down to 1) power samples and NO variance characterization, plus a provably false 'mean power confirms saturation' integrity sentence. A decision-maker would reasonably be misled about the trustworthiness of the finer distinctions and the saturation claim. The proposed fix (>=3 runs, median±spread, extend/steady-state window, stop citing power-mean-as-saturation) is appropriate. It is NOT a refutation of the top-line TPW or spec-decode conclusions, which survive; hence material, not a finding that overturns the report.

lenses.summary: All headline arithmetic reproduces exactly from the JSON artifacts: TPW ratios (fp8@300 38.18/18.08 = 2.11x), tok/W = tok_s/power for every run, spec-decode ratios (3.40/0.78/1.01/0.61x), and PPL deltas (+0.38%/+4.46%) all verified. The token-event count (19048) reproduces from the seeded RNG, and min==max==ignore_eos makes every config do identical work — a clean design. The report is also genuinely honest in listing 4 gaps and labeling spec-decode dead under load. The problems are methodological, and they cluster on the single most decision-relevant claim: that "TPW 2.11x HOLDS under saturated realistic load." The "saturated" regime is a 1.5–2.6 second burst that is ~31% prefill tokens and in which the GPU draws only 48–75% of the 700W cap — i.e. it is neither steady-state-decode nor power-saturated, the two conditions a real TPW-under-load claim needs. No trial is repeated (single shot each; "K" is spec tokens, not reps), so the load-bearing single-user spec number comes from one 0.12s/100-token run. The spec arm is additionally confounded by a different cudagraph capture set than the non-spec arm. The quality verdict ("4-bit unacceptable") rests on 185 teacher-forced tokens over 3 hand-picked passages with no variance and no downstream task — exactly the proxy-sufficiency risk the lens flags. The report's own gap list omits the two biggest uncovered risks: no thermal soak (the burst is too short for power/thermals to settle) and no long-context/KV-dominated regime (where FP8's weight-byte advantage shrinks and TPW 2x is most likely to break).

findings.title: "Saturated load" is a sub-2s burst that is ~31% prefill and never power-saturates — undercuts the central TPW-generalizes claim

Re-run with a sustained closed-loop arrival stream (e.g. 60-120s, refilling the batch) so decode dominates and power reaches steady state, then re-report tok/W. At minimum, disclose that the burst is ~31% prefill and draws well below the 700W cap, and soften "2.11x HOLDS under saturated load" to "2.11x in a ~2s prefill-heavy burst."

findings.title: No thermal soak and no long-context test — the two conditions most likely to break TPW 2x are untested AND missing from the gap list
findings.report_claim: Remaining gaps (lines 75-80) list only: substrate not loaded, batch-submit not Poisson, single GPU, short-to-mid context. Headline: TPW 2x "survived stress."

The gap list mentions short context as one of four bullets but does not connect it to TPW: in long-context decode, KV-cache bytes (fp16, unquantized) dominate the per-step byte budget, so FP8's weight-byte savings shrink and the FP8 throughput edge (already eroding 1.53x->1.36x, Result 3) likely collapses — directly threatening the 2.11x. The directive explicitly asked whether sustained thermal throttling and KV-dominated context could break TPW 2x; neither was tested.

The report asserts TPW 2x "✅ YES / survived stress (and improved)" with NO caveat tying it to the tested short-context, sub-soak regime — so a deployment decision-maker would over-generalize the 2.11x. Decision-relevant => material.

Minor downgrade on one sub-claim: the finding's headline says both conditions are "missing from the gap list." That is fully true for thermal soak, but long-context IS named in gap bullet #4 ("no long-context (where KV-cache, not weights, dominates the byte budget)"). The finding's own evidence text correctly concedes this ("mentions short context ... but does not connect it to TPW"), so the substantive point — long-context is present but NOT flagged as a TPW risk, and thermal soak is wholly absent — holds. Net: the finding is correct and material; only the word "missing" overstates slightly for long-context. The proposed fix (add thermal-soak gap; explicitly flag long-context/KV-dominated as the highest-risk uncovered TPW condition; mark 2.11x unproven for both) is appropriate.

finding.title: No repeated trials anywhere — every data point is a single shot; the load-bearing single-user spec number is one 0.12s run
finding.report_claim: Result 4: spec-decode "HELPS" at NREQ=1 with "3.40x"; conclusion "single-user / low-load LATENCY optimization." Result 1 TPW 2.11x.
finding.evidence: stress_driver.py has no repetition loop; ST_K ("K") is num_speculative_tokens (line 33), not trial count. sweep_fp8spec_n1.json: wall_s=0.12, total_gen_tokens=100, pw_samples=1, mean_power_w=null. The 3.40x = 857.6/252.6 comes from comparing a single 0.12s run to a single 0.4s run. Sub-0.5s vLLM timings are dominated by scheduler/launch noise; no variance is reported for any number in the report.
finding.suggested_fix: Report >=3 trials with mean and spread for at least the headline TPW configs and the spec sweep. Flag the N=1 spec point as a 0.12s single-shot measurement and do not present 3.40x as a precise figure. The qualitative conclusion (spec helps single-user, hurts under load) likely survives, but the specific multipliers do not warrant 2-3 significant figures.

verdict.reasoning:
Fully confirmed against artifacts. stress_driver.py runs llm.generate() exactly once per config (line 60) with a single warmup (line 56); there is no repetition loop, no median/mean-over-trials, no stdev anywhere. ST_K (line 10) is num_speculative_tokens (line 33), not a trial count, exactly as the finding states. The load-bearing single-user spec number is genuinely one 0.12s run: sweep_fp8spec_n1.json has wall_s=0.12, total_gen_tokens=100, pw_samples=1, mean_power_w=null. The report's headline 3.40x (line 48) = 857.6/252.6 = 3.395x, comparing this single 0.12s run to a single 0.40s run (sweep_fp8_n1.json, wall_s=0.4). All other points are also single-shot (six st_*.json saturated runs + three sweep pairs, each one generate() call). grep of the report for trial/±/std/stdev/variance/median/error-bar returns nothing — no spread is reported for any number.

Material because the report presents 3.40x and 0.61-1.01x to 2-3 sig figs and builds Result 4's conclusion partly on the noisiest possible measurement (~120ms wall, where vLLM scheduler/launch/cudagraph-warmup overhead can swing tens of percent). A decision-maker would over-trust a precise multiplier with zero measured variance.

One downgrade-pressure caveat that I verified but that does NOT save the precision problem: the qualitative direction ("spec hurts under load") is independently corroborated by the larger-token, lower-noise runs — NREQ=4 at 0.78x (392 tokens) and NREQ=128 at 0.61x (19048 tokens, st_fp8_spec/st_fp8_base = 7877.4/12906.0 = 0.610x). So the finding's defect is precisely the single-shot/over-precise framing of the multipliers (especially the 3.40x headline), not the qualitative conclusion — which is exactly what the finding itself claims. Hence: refuted=false, material.

finding.title: Quality verdict ("4-bit unacceptable, FP8 dominates on quality") rests on 185 teacher-forced tokens over 3 passages, no variance, no downstream task
finding.report_claim: Result 2: "now MEASURED"; "4-bit's is 12x larger (+4.46%)"; "FP8 dominates 4-bit on every axis ... AND quality"; scorecard: quality "now measured / real."
finding.evidence: ppl_*.json: n_tokens=185 for all three arms; quality_ppl.py uses exactly 3 short encyclopedia/textbook passages (texts[] lines 13-16), teacher-forced prompt_logprobs, single run, no CI. A +4.46% PPL delta on 185 in-distribution tokens has a wide confidence interval and does not establish downstream-task failure. Additional confound: the fp16 baseline log shows "Casting torch.bfloat16 to torch.float16" (Mistral-7B-v0.1 is native bf16), so the fp16 reference is itself a downcast, while gptq is a third-party requant of a different checkpoint (TheBloke/Mistral-7B-v0.1-GPTQ, stress_driver.py line 31 / quality_ppl.py line 10).
finding.suggested_fix: Downgrade "4-bit is unacceptable" to "PPL proxy suggests 4-bit degrades ~10x more than FP8; needs a real downstream-accuracy eval (e.g. MMLU/GSM8K/HumanEval subset) on hundreds-to-thousands of tokens before concluding unacceptable." Note the bf16->fp16 cast and the different GPTQ checkpoint as confounds in the quality comparison.
finding.location: R_STRESS_TEST_2026-06-11.md lines 27-37, 70-73; ppl_fp16.json/ppl_fp8.json/ppl_gptq.json; quality_ppl.py lines 7-19; ppl_fp16.log

verdict.reasoning:
Verified every artifact claim in the finding and it holds fully.

CONFIRMED AGAINST ARTIFACTS:
- ppl_fp16.json/ppl_fp8.json/ppl_gptq.json all report n_tokens=185 (identical for all three arms).
- quality_ppl.py texts[] (lines 13-16) = exactly 3 short encyclopedia/textbook passages (mitochondrion, Apollo 11, transformer). Single run; grep for ci/std/variance/bootstrap/repeat/confidence/trial/n_runs returns nothing — no variance, no CI, no downstream task.
- Deltas re-derived from raw JSON: FP8 +0.38%, GPTQ +4.46%, ratio = 11.73x (report says "12x larger" — fine, the rounded report values 3.405/3.544 give 12.6x). Arithmetic is correct.
- bf16->fp16 cast confound is REAL: ppl_fp16.log line 1 = "WARNING ... [model.py:2018] Casting torch.bfloat16 to torch.float16." Mistral-7B-v0.1 is native bf16. Crucially, ppl_fp8.log and ppl_gptq.log show NO such cast — so the fp16 *reference* is itself a downcast and the asymmetry is one-sided (only the baseline arm is downcast), directly affecting the headline deltas everything is measured against.
- GPTQ checkpoint confound is REAL: quality_ppl.py line 10 / stress_driver.py line 31 load TheBloke/Mistral-7B-v0.1-GPTQ (third-party requant) for the gptq arm, vs mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1 for fp16/fp8. So part of the "4-bit penalty" may be checkpoint provenance, not quantization precision.
- Report DISCLOSURE: grep of R_STRESS_TEST shows it discloses NONE of these — no mention of bf16 cast, different GPTQ checkpoint, absence of variance/CI, or downstream-task limitation. It states (lines 36-37) "FP8 dominates 4-bit on every axis ... AND quality" and the scorecard (line 70) flips quality from "hand-waved" to "now measured", with the conclusion (line 73) "Quality is now real."

SEVERITY: Material. The report converts a thin, confounded PPL proxy (185 in-distribution tokens, no CI, downcast baseline, mismatched 4-bit checkpoint) into a settled, headline quality axis ("now real", "dominates on every axis AND quality") that the overall recommendation — "TPW/MBU wins should ride on FP8, not 4-bit" — explicitly leans on. A decision-maker would over-trust this verdict and treat 4-bit as quality-disqualified. The directional ranking (4-bit degrades ~10x more) is plausible and probably survives the confounds, so the finding is NOT that the conclusion is wrong — it is that the strength/finality is overstated and the confounds are undisclosed. That is exactly what makes it misleading rather than merely a wording nit. The proposed fix (downgrade to "PPL proxy suggests ~10x more degradation; needs a real downstream eval"; disclose the bf16->fp16 cast and the different GPTQ checkpoint) is correct and proportionate.

Not refuted: I could not find anything in the artifacts that rehabilitates the "now real / dominates on quality" framing — no larger token set, no repeated runs, no native-precision baseline, no downstream eval exists in the evidence.

finding.title: Spec-decode conclusion is confounded: spec arm uses a different (truncated) cudagraph capture set than the non-spec arm, and uses ngram not a real draft model
finding.report_claim: Result 4: "spec-decode is a single-user / low-load LATENCY optimization, NOT a server-throughput lever" — concluded from spec-vs-no-spec throughput ratios.
finding.evidence: stress_driver.py line 34: when SPEC, compilation_config sets cudagraph_capture_sizes=[8,16,24,32] only; the non-spec arm (line 27) uses vLLM defaults (which capture much larger sizes). At NREQ=128 the decode batch far exceeds 32, so the spec arm runs uncaptured/eager for large batches while non-spec is fully captured — a graph-capture penalty independent of speculation that inflates the apparent "spec hurts." Separately, method=ngram/prompt-lookup (line 33) is not a trained draft model; the directive asked whether a real draft model behaves differently, which is untested and unaddressed.
finding.suggested_fix: Re-run the spec arm with the same cudagraph capture configuration as the non-spec baseline (or both eager) to isolate the speculation effect. Add a caveat that the conclusion is for ngram prompt-lookup spec only; a trained draft model has a different draft cost/acceptance profile and is not covered.

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED as material. Both halves of the finding hold against the artifacts.

(A) Cudagraph capture-set asymmetry — REAL and decisive. stress_driver.py line 34 sets cudagraph_capture_sizes=[8,16,24,32] ONLY when SPEC, while the non-spec arm (line 27) uses vLLM defaults. The .err artifacts prove the asymmetry directly: every non-spec run (st_fp8_base.err, sweep_fp8_n1/n4/n16.err, st_gptq_pl300.err, st_fp16_base.err) shows "Capturing CUDA graphs ... 0/51" = 51 captured graph sizes; the spec run st_fp8_spec.err shows "0/3" = only 3. With ngram K=5 the FULL-decode graph must cover running_seqs*(K+1)=6 verified tokens/seq, so the truncated [8,16,24,32] set fails to cover NREQ=16 (~96 tokens) and NREQ=128 (~768 tokens) — exactly the saturated points the verdict rests on. There the spec arm runs uncaptured/eager while the non-spec baseline is fully captured, a graph-capture penalty independent of speculation. The report nowhere mentions cudagraph/capture/eager (grep returns nothing), so the confound is undisclosed. Conclusion "Spec-decode ... NOT a server-throughput lever ... does not survive a loaded server" (lines 43-56) and scorecard "❌ NO (single-user only)" (line 68) are drawn from contaminated NREQ>=16 comparisons.

Skeptical nuance (kept honest, does not rescue the report): at NREQ=1 (spec batch 6) and NREQ=4 (spec batch 24) BOTH arms are effectively captured, so the 3.40x win at N=1 and the 0.78x dip at N=4 are NOT capture-confounded. So the report's broad observation that spec only helps at very low load has some clean support, but the headline saturated numbers (N=16 neutral 1.01x, N=128 -39%) — which carry the verdict — are exactly the confounded ones. This makes the finding material, not a total refutation of every cell.

(B) ngram vs trained draft model — REAL, smaller. Line 33 method=ngram (prompt-lookup), not a trained draft model. Report labels the table "ngram-spec" (line 44) but Result 4 and the scorecard generalize to "Spec-decode 2x+ ... single-user only" without restricting to ngram. A trained draft has a different draft-cost/acceptance profile, untested and unaddressed. The arithmetic ratios all reproduce exactly from JSON (857.6/252.6=3.40, 599.4/766.7=0.78, 1854.4/1835.8=1.01, 7877.4/12906=0.61), so the numbers are right but the methodology behind the headline conclusion is confounded and over-generalized. A decision-maker reading "spec-decode is not a server lever" could wrongly abandon spec-decode when the loaded result is partly a self-inflicted capture handicap and is specific to ngram.

finding.title: Spec curve is non-monotonic and the workload mix changes across sweep points, so 'clean collapse at NREQ>=4' overstates the data
finding.report_claim: Result 4 (line 53): 'At any realistic concurrency (NREQ>=4) spec-decode is neutral-to-negative.' Table lines 48-51 list 3.40x / 0.78x / 1.01x / 0.61x.
finding.evidence: The curve is non-monotonic: NREQ=4=0.78x (hurts), NREQ=16=1.01x (neutral, i.e. NOT hurting), NREQ=128=0.61x (hurts). Worse, the sweep points are not the same workload: reproducing the seeded rng, NREQ=1 is a SINGLE RAG/verbatim-copy prompt (the best case for ngram spec), NREQ=4 adds 2 chat + 1 instruct, NREQ=16 is 3 rag / 6 instruct / 5 chat / 2 code, NREQ=128 is 19/39/39/31. So the ratio swings reflect changing task mix AND tiny token counts (n4=392 tok over 0.51-0.65s; n1=100 tok over 0.12s, single power sample, mean_power null in sweep_fp8spec_n1.json) as much as load. The data supports 'spec is not a server-throughput win,' but the specific monotone 'collapses as load rises' story is not clean.
finding.suggested_fix: Hold the task mix fixed across NREQ (or report per-task-type), increase token counts so the sub-second sweep points are stable, and describe the result as 'neutral-to-negative and noisy at concurrency, not a throughput lever' rather than a clean monotone collapse. Note NREQ=16=1.01x is neutral, not harmful.

verdict.reasoning:
All four spec ratios reproduce exactly from the JSONs (857.6/252.6=3.40; 599.4/766.7=0.78; 1854.4/1835.8=1.01; 7877.4/12906.0=0.61). The finding is correct that (a) the curve is non-monotonic (0.78 dips, 1.01 recovers to neutral, 0.61 dips again) and (b) the workload mix changes across sweep points — I reproduced the seeded RNG faithfully (forced output-token sums match total_gen_tokens exactly: 100/392/1924/19048), confirming NREQ=1 is 100% rag (best case for ngram spec) diluting to a mixed bag at NREQ=128. Low-NREQ points are also thin (n1=100 tok/0.12s/pw_samples:1/mean_power_w:null, confirmed).

However, the finding's load-bearing claim — that the report tells a 'clean collapse'/'clean monotone collapses as load rises' story that overstates the data — is refuted by the report's actual text. grep confirms 'collapse' and 'monotone' appear NOWHERE in the report; they are the finding author's paraphrase. The report explicitly labels NREQ=16 as 'neutral' in its table (line 50), states the conclusion as 'neutral-to-negative' (line 53-54), and gives the range '0.61–1.01×' in the scorecard (line 68) — all of which already disclose the non-monotonicity and include the neutral point. The finding's own recommended FIX ('describe as neutral-to-negative and noisy, not a clean monotone collapse') is essentially what the report already says. So the finding attacks a strawman framing the report did not adopt.

The residual valid sub-points (mix not held fixed; tiny low-NREQ token counts) are real but minor: the headline decision-relevant point is the saturated NREQ=128 result (0.61x, 19048 tokens each, identical SEED⇒identical mix between spec and base arms, 12-20 power samples), which is robust and apples-to-apples; the mix-shift actually strengthens the report's claim that NREQ=1's high ratio is a best-case artifact. The finding's own per-bucket mix counts are also inaccurate (claimed n4=2chat+1instruct vs actual 1/1/1/1; n16=3/6/5/2 vs actual 5/5/4/2; n128=19/39/39/31 vs actual 30/36/39/23). Net: the report's wording is already appropriately hedged and the core conclusion a decision-maker acts on (spec is single-user-only, not a server-throughput lever) is sound. Not a finding.
